title: Fitting a single model
text:
bayesnec fits concentration-response curves to toxicity data and derives no-effect concentration (NEC), no-significant-effect concentration (NSEC, Fisher and Fox (2023)) and effect concentration (ECx) estimates from non-linear models fitted by Bayesian Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, via brms (Bürkner 2017; Bürkner 2018) and Stan. It is an extension of jagsNEC (Fisher et al. 2020).
This module fits one model to one dataset and works through everything that can be done with the result: checking that it converged, looking inside the fitted object, plotting it, and extracting toxicity estimates. Later modules cover the full model set, model averaging, the choice of statistical distribution, and priors.
If you have not yet installed R, a C++ compiler, CmdStan and bayesnec, work through the software setup first. Nothing in this module will run without them.

If you have not yet installed R, a C++ compiler, CmdStan and bayesnec, work through the software setup first. Nothing in this module will run without them.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
The example dataset
bayesnec supplies a small example dataset, nec_data, with two columns: x, the concentration, and y, the response.

library(bayesnec)
data(nec_data)
head(nec_data)

          x         y
1 1.0187462 0.8602703
2 0.8157475 0.9102426
3 0.3713305 0.8485031
4 0.4008323 0.9226047
5 1.2945451 0.8657107
6 1.3897943 0.9163264


The response here is a proportion bounded by zero and one, which matters for the statistical distribution used to model it. bayesnec will choose a distribution from the characteristics of the data unless told otherwise, and module 5 covers that choice in full.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Reproducibility
A Bayesian model is fitted by drawing samples, so running the same code twice gives slightly different numbers unless the random number generator is set to a known state. set.seed() does that, and every fit in this course is preceded by one.

set.seed(333)

The estimates below will not match yours to the last decimal place unless you use the same seed, the same number of chains and the same version of the package. They should match to within the width of the credible intervals, and if they do not, that is worth investigating rather than accepting.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
The bnec function
bnec is the working function of the package. It assembles the non-linear model formula, generates priors and initial values, and calls brms. It is designed for an R user who is comfortable with model-fitting syntax but is not a specialist in non-linear or Bayesian modelling.
Run ?bnec for the full argument list. Beyond the formula and the data, the arguments fall into four groups: the model or model set to fit (model); how toxicity estimates are computed from the fit (x_range, resolution, sig_val); how the response and predictor are identified when the formula alone is not enough (x_var, y_var, trials_var); and how priors are set (prior, prior_type).
Anything else is passed through to brms::brm() by ..., so the full brm argument list is available. Three brm arguments are worth knowing about because bayesnec sets them differently from brms. It generates its own family and prior values rather than using the brms defaults, and it raises the number of iterations from 2,000 to 10,000, with a correspondingly longer warm-up, because the non-linear models here often need it.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
The formula
A bayesnec formula takes the form:

y ~ crf(x, model = "modelname")

The left-hand side is the response, exactly as in brms. The right-hand side uses crf(), a function specific to bayesnec, which stands for concentration-response function. It takes the predictor and the name of the model to fit, and it accepts a transformation of the predictor, such as crf(log(x), ...).
Term names must match the columns of the data frame exactly, as in any R formula.
The available models are:

models()$all

 [1] "nec3param"     "nec4param"     "nechorme"      "nechorme4"    
 [5] "necsigm"       "neclin"        "neclinhorme"   "nechormepwr"  
 [9] "nechorme4pwr"  "nechormepwr01" "ecxlin"        "ecxexp"       
[13] "ecxsigm"       "ecx4param"     "ecxwb1"        "ecxwb2"       
[17] "ecxwb1p3"      "ecxwb2p3"      "ecxll5"        "ecxll4"       
[21] "ecxll3"        "ecxhormebc4"   "ecxhormebc5"  


These fall into named groups, which is how a set of models is requested rather than a single one:

names(models())

[1] "nec"          "ecx"          "all"          "bot_free"     "zero_bounded"
[6] "decline"      "hormesis"    


Module 3 describes what each model does and which toxicity estimates follow from it. Module 4 covers fitting a set rather than a single model.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Calling bnec
Supplying a formula and a data frame is enough; everything else takes a default.

set.seed(333)
bnec_fit <- bnec(y ~ crf(x, model = "nec3param"), data = nec_data)

Finding initial values which allow the response to be fitted using a nec3param model and a beta distribution.


Compiling Stan program...


Start sampling


Response variable modelled as a nec3param model using a beta distribution.


Warning: Found 1 observations with a pareto_k > 0.7 in model 'nec3param'. We
recommend to set 'moment_match = TRUE' in order to perform moment matching for
problematic observations.


Warning: 
2 (2.0%) p_waic estimates greater than 0.4. We recommend trying loo instead.


The first thing that happens is compilation. Stan models are written in the Stan language, translated to C++ and compiled to a shared object, which R then loads and runs. This is why the first fit of a session is slower than later ones, and why a compiler is needed at all.
Sampling follows. How long the whole thing takes depends on the machine, the number of chains and the number of iterations. The fit above took a little over two minutes on four cores. Use at least as many cores as you have chains:

options(mc.cores = 4)

More cores than chains gives no benefit without additional configuration.
When the fit completes, bayesnec reports which model was fitted and which statistical distribution was used. Here it is a nec3param model with a beta distribution.
Warnings may also appear. The two above concern the Pareto k diagnostic and p_waic, both of which relate to the leave-one-out cross-validation used to compute model weights. Weights are irrelevant when a single model has been fitted, and module 4 returns to them when they are not.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Saving the fit
A fitted model is expensive to produce and cheap to store, so save it as soon as it finishes.

saveRDS(bnec_fit, "nec3param_fit.rds")
bnec_fit <- readRDS("nec3param_fit.rds")

Be deliberate about where. This is one of the smallest fits in the course and the object is 5.2 Mb, because it stores every posterior draw for every parameter. A model-averaged set of all 23 models is very much larger, and a fit to real data with a grouping variable larger again. A folder synchronised by OneDrive or a similar service is a poor choice: the upload is slow, and on some configurations it interferes with writing the file at all.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
The summary

summary(bnec_fit)

Object of class bayesnecfit containing the nec3param model

 Family: beta 
  Links: mu = identity 
Formula: y ~ top * exp(-exp(beta) * (x - nec) * step(x - nec)) 
         top ~ 1
         beta ~ 1
         nec ~ 1
   Data: data (Number of observations: 100) 
  Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 10000; warmup = 8000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 8000

Regression Coefficients:
     Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
top      0.89      0.01     0.88     0.90 1.00     6722     5305
beta     0.54      0.06     0.42     0.66 1.00     5266     4623
nec      1.53      0.02     1.50     1.57 1.00     5786     4930

Further Distributional Parameters:
    Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
phi    52.03      7.61    38.22    67.79 1.00     6708     5424

Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

    Estimate Q2.5 Q97.5
NEC     1.53 1.50  1.57


Bayesian R2 estimates:
   Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5
R2     0.96      0.00 0.96  0.97


There is a lot here, and each part is worth reading.
The object is of class bayesnecfit, containing the nec3param model. bayesnec returns a bayesnecfit when one model is fitted, and a bayesmanecfit when a set is fitted.
The family is the beta distribution with an identity link. This is deliberate and it is not the brms default, which for a beta response is the logit. bayesnec uses the identity link for every family, so that the top, bot and nec parameters stay on the scale of the response and remain directly interpretable. It matters if you ever compare a bayesnec fit against a brm model you have written yourself: unless you pass the link explicitly, the two are different models.
The brms formula that was actually fitted is printed. For nec3param it is a constant top until the concentration reaches nec, followed by exponential decay, with the switch implemented by step(). Module 3 sets out the equations.
Rhat is a convergence diagnostic and should be close to 1. All three parameters here are at 1.00, and the effective sample sizes are in the thousands, both of which indicate the sampler explored the posterior properly.
The NEC estimate is given below the coefficients, as a median with a 95% credible interval, and the Bayesian R² gives an indication of fit. The value here is high, as you would expect of a simulated example where the curve is well-determined; real data rarely look this tidy.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Checking the fit
brms offers a range of diagnostics, and the brms documentation covers them far better than this course can. Extract the underlying model with pull_brmsfit():

brm_fit <- pull_brmsfit(bnec_fit)

Plotting it gives the marginal posterior of each parameter beside its trace:

plot(brm_fit)








Read the traces from left to right. Four chains that overlap, with no drift and no sustained excursion, indicate the chains have converged on the same distribution. Chains that separate into bands, or wander, indicate they have not, and the estimates should not be used.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Inside the fitted object
A bayesnecfit is a list holding the brms fit and a set of derived quantities.

names(bnec_fit)

 [1] "fit"             "model"           "init"            "bayesnecformula"
 [5] "pred_vals"       "top"             "beta"            "ne"             
 [9] "f"               "bot"             "d"               "slope"          
[13] "ec50"            "dispersion"      "predicted_y"     "residuals"      
[17] "ne_posterior"    "ne_type"        


pred_vals holds fitted values across the range of the predictor, which is what the plotting methods use and what you would use for a custom figure:

head(bnec_fit$pred_vals$data)

           x  Estimate      Q2.5     Q97.5
1 0.03234801 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465
2 0.03553938 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465
3 0.03873074 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465
4 0.04192210 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465
5 0.04511347 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465
6 0.04830483 0.8890547 0.8786256 0.8986465


Every fitted model carries a posterior for the no-effect estimate, in ne_posterior, with ne_type recording what kind of estimate it is. For models in the nec group this is the posterior of the nec parameter itself. For models in the ecx group, which have no threshold parameter, it is the posterior of the NSEC (Fisher and Fox 2023). Module 3 explains why those are different things.

hist(bnec_fit$ne_posterior,
     main = "", xlab = "No-effect concentration", col = "grey80", border = "white")

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Plotting
plot() extends the base method and autoplot() extends the ggplot2 method. Both take arguments controlling what is drawn; see ?autoplot.bayesnecfit.

autoplot(bnec_fit) +
  ggplot2::xlab("Concentration")

Ignoring unknown labels:
• fill : "NA"
• colour : "NA"









The result is a ggplot object, so it composes with + in the usual way, and most ggplot2 functions will work on it.
By default the plot is annotated with the fitted no-effect estimate and its 95% credible interval, and labelled with the model that was fitted. The annotation is labelled N(S)EC, because the same plotting code serves both model groups. For a nec3param fit the quantity is an NEC, and it is worth relabelling it as such in anything you present.

title: Fitting a single model
text:
Toxicity estimates
Three functions extract estimates from a fitted model: ecx(), nec() and nsec().

ecx(bnec_fit)

     Q50     Q2.5    Q97.5 
1.596282 1.563494 1.626652 
attr(,"resolution")
[1] 200
attr(,"ecx_val")
[1] 10
attr(,"toxicity_estimate")
[1] "ecx"

nec(bnec_fit)

     Q50     Q2.5    Q97.5 
1.534924 1.497388 1.569384 
attr(,"toxicity_estimate")
[1] "nec"

nsec(bnec_fit)

Warning: The nec3param curve does not fall below the control's 0.01 quantile
anywhere in the predictor range for 80 of 8000 draws, which return NA. The NSEC
is censored above 3.22.


     Q50     Q2.5    Q97.5 
1.542647 1.507051 1.575059 
attr(,"resolution")
[1] 200
attr(,"sig_val")
[1] 0.01
attr(,"toxicity_estimate")
[1] "nsec"
attr(,"ecnsec_relativeP")
      50%      2.5%     97.5% 
1.4135682 0.2433627 2.4658367 


Each returns a median and a 95% probability interval by default, and each records how it was computed in the attributes of the returned object: ecx() returns an EC10 unless told otherwise, and nsec() uses a significance value of 0.01.
For this dataset the three estimates are close together, which happens when the curve declines sharply from a well-defined threshold. They are not interchangeable, and on other data they separate widely. Module 3 covers what each of them measures and when each is appropriate.

title: Concentration-response modelling
text:
Estimates of no-effect toxicity underpin both risk assessment and the derivation of environmental quality standards. A range of statistical approaches developed or adopted in ecotoxicology over the past decade have changed how those estimates are obtained from concentration-response experiments, and this course covers the current methods for deriving them in R.
The material begins with concentration-response modelling itself: the difference between linear, non-linear and threshold models, the natural scale of a response variable and what follows from it for the choice of statistical distribution, and the distinction between the toxicity metrics that can be derived from a fitted curve. It then introduces the no-significant-effect concentration (NSEC), and works through fitting and interpretation using bayesnec, which fits these models in a Bayesian framework via brms and Stan. Model averaging is treated throughout rather than as an addition, because a single equation chosen from a candidate set rarely carries the evidence a guideline value needs.

title: Concentration-response modelling
text:
Working through the material independently
The modules are written to be read in order and are self-contained. Each shows the code that produced every result on the page, so the reasoning can be followed without running anything.
Fitting Bayesian concentration-response models takes time. A single model may take minutes and a model-averaged set considerably longer, so the larger fits in these modules are shown with their code and their output rather than being run as you read. Anything that runs quickly is intended to be run.
If you want to run the code yourself, work through the software setup first. It installs R, a C++ compiler, CmdStan and the R packages, and ends with a script that verifies the installation.

title: Concentration-response modelling
text:
Workshop participants
This material is taught as a full-day workshop at SETAC Australasia 2026.
The software setup is pre-work and must be completed beforehand. No time is set aside on the day to install or repair software, and a participant without a working installation will be able to follow the demonstrations but not fit models alongside them.

title: Concentration-response modelling
text:
Source and citation
The material is developed at the Australian Institute of Marine Science and the source is at open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training.
bayesnec is documented at open-aims.github.io/bayesnec. The NSEC is introduced in Fisher and Fox (2023), Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry.
Corrections and questions are welcome as issues.

title: Software setup
text:
ImportantComplete this before the workshop



This setup takes most people between thirty minutes and two hours, and some of it cannot be hurried: package installation and the CmdStan build both take time that depends on your machine and your network.
There is no time set aside during the workshop to install or repair software. If you arrive without a working installation you will be able to watch, but you will not be able to fit models alongside the demonstrations, and most of the day is spent fitting models.
Work through this document, then run the verification check in the final section and send the output to the organisers. Doing that early leaves time for a problem to be resolved before the day.

title: Software setup
text:
Software required



Software
Purpose




R
the language everything else runs in


A C++ toolchain
compiles each Bayesian model before it is fitted


CmdStan
the sampler that fits the models


Positron
the editor used throughout the workshop


Git
retrieves the workshop materials



The C++ toolchain is the part that differs by operating system, and it is the part that fails most often. On Windows it is Rtools, on macOS the Xcode Command Line Tools, and on Linux the standard build tools.
Bayesian model fitting works differently from most R modelling. Each model is translated into C++, compiled into a program, and run. That is why a compiler is needed at all, and why the first fit of a session takes longer than later ones.

title: Software setup
text:
Route by operating system
Windows is the tested and recommended route, and it is the one described in most detail below. The difficulties Stan had on Windows historically came from an older interface, rstan, which required matched versions of several compiled packages. The current interface, cmdstanr, avoids most of that.
Linux is also tested. macOS is not, because the workshop organisers have no Mac available. Mac users should follow the outline in the macOS section, which points to the authoritative upstream instructions, and then run the same verification check as everyone else. The check is what determines whether you are ready, not which instructions you followed.
The Windows Subsystem for Linux is a fallback for one situation only, described in its own section. Do not start there.

title: Software setup
text:
R and Rtools
Install R first, then Rtools.
Download R from CRAN. The combination tested for this workshop is R 4.5.x.
Then install Rtools45, from CRAN’s Rtools page. Accept the default installation location.






WarningRtools must match your version of R



Rtools45 is for R 4.5.x. A different R minor version needs the matching Rtools: Rtools44 for R 4.4.x, and so on. A mismatch is the most common single cause of setup failure, and the error it produces does not mention version numbers.
If you install a version of R other than 4.5.x, install the Rtools that matches it.

title: Software setup
text:
Positron
Download and install Positron. It will find your R installation automatically. If you installed R after Positron, restart Positron so that it detects it.

title: Software setup
text:
Git
Install Git for Windows, accepting the defaults. Git is used to retrieve the workshop materials.

title: Software setup
text:
R packages
Open Positron and run the following in the R console.
cmdstanr is not on CRAN, so it comes from the Stan project’s own repository:
install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                           getOption("repos")))
Then the rest:
install.packages(c("brms", "posterior", "bayesplot",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "drc"))
brms installs rstan as a dependency. That is expected. rstan must be installed, but the workshop does not use it as the sampler, so it does not matter if you never call it directly.






NoteThe bayesnec version



The workshop teaches a specific version of bayesnec, and the functions that estimate toxicity values changed in it. Installing a different version will give you different results from the ones on screen.
[TO BE CONFIRMED BEFORE THIS DOCUMENT IS ISSUED — do not send with this placeholder in place. The exact install command and version follow the release planned for Monday.]

title: Software setup
text:
CmdStan
First confirm the compiler is configured. fix = TRUE repairs the common problems rather than only reporting them:
cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)
Then install CmdStan. Give it a plain installation path, rather than accepting the default:
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(dir = "C:/cmdstan")
The default location is inside your home directory. On many Windows machines, particularly work-managed ones, that directory is synchronised by OneDrive, and the CmdStan build fails there. The same failure occurs when the path contains a space or a character outside the standard English alphabet, which happens when a Windows username does. Installing to C:/cmdstan avoids all three, and costs nothing if none of them applies to you.
Because that is not the default location, tell R where to find it in every future session. Run usethis::edit_r_profile(), or open .Rprofile in your home directory, and add the line below, replacing the version number with the one you installed:
options(cmdstanr_cmdstan_path = "C:/cmdstan/cmdstan-2.39.0")
Without this, every new session reports that CmdStan is not installed.

Recurring problems on Windows
install_cmdstan() fails. Run it again with these arguments:
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, quiet = FALSE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")
This is the failure most recently observed on a fresh Windows machine, and this is what resolved it. overwrite = TRUE is the part that matters. A first attempt that fails partway through the build leaves a partly built directory behind, and a second attempt without overwrite declines to replace it, which produces an error resembling the original one. quiet = FALSE only prints more of the build output, which is worth having because the default output is truncated and does not identify which stage failed.
A model compiles but no chains run. cmdstanr reports “No chains finished successfully”, which names neither a cause nor a file. On Windows a compiled Stan program loads tbb.dll from CmdStan’s own library directory as it starts, and if that directory is not on the PATH the program exits immediately. Add it:
# adjust the version number to the one you installed
"C:/cmdstan/cmdstan-2.39.0/stan/lib/stan_math/lib/tbb"
install_cmdstan() normally adds this entry, so a missing one indicates that step did not complete. check_setup.R reports on it directly. This was found on a Windows machine during preparation of this course, and it is the reason the check script compiles the example afresh on every run rather than reusing an existing executable.
Compiling is very slow. Windows Defender inspects each newly compiled program. A compile that should take under a minute can take several. Excluding the C:/cmdstan directory from real-time scanning resolves it, where your organisation’s policy allows.
Compiling is blocked entirely. Some managed machines prevent newly compiled programs from running at all. This is a policy decision rather than a configuration problem and cannot be worked around from within R. See the Windows Subsystem for Linux section.






TipTime box the native route



Give the steps above about thirty minutes. If the verification check passes, stop. If compilation fails for reasons of security policy rather than something you can configure, move to WSL rather than continuing to adjust settings.

title: Software setup
text:
Reporting the result
Copy the entire output, from the first line to the last, and send it to the organisers. Send it whether it passed or failed: a passing result confirms you are ready, and a failing one gives enough detail to identify the problem in advance.
The output contains your R version, your operating system, your package versions and your installation paths. It contains nothing else about your machine.
Send it as early as you can. A problem found a week before the workshop can be resolved; the same problem found on the morning cannot.
